title: How to Reduce Sequence-of-Returns Risk in Early Retirement
description: Protecting your portfolio from a market crash in the 'Fragile Decade'.
content:
The greatest risk to a retiree isn't running out of money at 90; it's running out of money at 65 because the market crashed the year they retired. This is **Sequence of Returns Risk**. If your portfolio drops 20% in Year 1 of retirement and you withdraw 4% for living expenses, you dig a hole so deep that even a subsequent bull market cannot dig you out. Mathematically, the order of your investment returns matters just as much as the average return. This guide explains defensive strategies like 'Bond Tents' and 'Cash Buffers' to survive the danger zone.

Key Takeaways

  • The Danger Zone: The 5 years before and 5 years after retirement are critical. A crash here has a devastating multiplier effect on portfolio longevity.
  • The 'Bond Tent': A strategy where you ramp up your bond/cash allocation to its peak (e.g., 60%) right at retirement, then slowly spend it down, drifting back into stocks over 10 years. This shields you during the most vulnerable moment.
  • Dynamic Withdrawals: The ability to cut spending. If the market drops, skipping an inflation adjustment or cutting 'fun money' prevents you from selling depreciated assets.
  • Cash Buffer: Holding 2 years of expenses in pure cash allows you to ignore the stock market for 24 months. You spend the cash, not the stocks.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The S&P 500 has historically recovered from bear markets in ~2-3 years (on average). A cash buffer of 3 years allows you to bridge almost any historical recession without selling equities at a loss.

The Math of a Bad Start

Two retirees start with $1 Million and withdraw $40,000/year.

Retiree A: The Lucky One

Year 1 Return: +20%.
Year 2 Return: -10%.
Result: Portfolio grows. The early gain buffers the withdrawal.

Retiree B: The Unlucky One (Sequence Risk)

Year 1 Return: -20%.
Balance drops to $800k. Withdrawing $40k is now 5% of the portfolio.
Year 2 Return: +10%.
Result: Even with the recovery, Retiree B is permanently behind. The principal was depleted while it was down. This 'Reverse Dollar Cost Averaging' is the portfolio killer.

The Guardrail

If Retiree B had a 'Bond Tent', they would have sold Bonds (which were stable) in Year 1, leaving their Stocks untouched to recover in Year 2.

Building the Defense

  1. 5 Years Out: Stop reinvesting dividends. Direct all new contributions to Cash and Short-Term Bonds. Shift allocation from 80/20 to 60/40 or 50/50.
  2. Retirement Day: Your portfolio should be at its most conservative point. You have 3-5 years of safe spending money in liquid assets.
  3. The Glide Path: In retirement, spend the bonds first. As you age, your stock percentage actually increases (Rising Equity Glidepath). This combats inflation late in life.
  4. Variable Spending Rule: 'If the market is down >10%, I do not take an inflation adjustment this year.' This simple rule increases portfolio survival rates from 80% to 98%.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is 100% cash safe?

No. That guarantees failure due to inflation. You need stocks for growth. You just need enough cash to survive the volatility of the stocks.

What is a CAPE ratio?

Cyclically Adjusted Price-to-Earnings. When CAPE is high (stocks are expensive), sequence of returns risk is higher. Be more conservative when retiring into a bull market peak.

Does working part-time help?

Immensely. Earning $20k/year prevents you from withdrawing $20k. It reduces the strain on the portfolio during the critical early years.
